entry.title: Wade’s rules part 1
entry.content:
I was doing some SciBowl sets a few days ago, and I came across something called “Wade’s rules”. I looked further into this, and it seems pretty cool. Wade’s rules let us predict the shapes of borane clusters. Their shape depends on the number of boron atoms (obviously) and the number of skeletal electron pairs (SEPs), electron pairs that aren’t part of a B-H bond. Let n denote the number of boron atoms, which will be the vertices of the resulting cluster. To start, if you have \(n\) vertices and \(n+1\) SEPs, you get something called a closo structure. This closo structure is the base we modify. From Wikipedia:

Vertices Polyhedron
4 Tetrahedron
5 Trigonal bipyramid
6 Octahedron
7 Pentagonal bipyramid
8 Snub disphenoid
9 Tricapped trigonal prism
10 Bicapped square antiprism

OK. Everything looks pretty normal except for the snub disphenoid?? Most of these look similar to VSEPR structures. Actually, this happens because there is a requirement for all faces to be triangular due to some MO interactions that I will go over in part 2. A normal VSEPR structure for a steric number of 8 is a square antiprism, which has square faces.

Now we can go on to changing \(n\) while keeping the number of SEPs the same. If we have $n-1$ sides, we remove a vertex and call it a nido structure. If we remove another vertex, it is an arachno structure. Removing one more gets us a hypho structure. Alternatively, to add vertices, we “cap” a triangular face with an additional vertex, which forms kind of a tetrahedron there.

Shown here is a great diagram to understand these structures. Now I was curious: where do these names come from? Turns out that closo means closed cage, nido means nest, arachno means spider’s web, and hypho means net. What an interesting naming scheme.

Another thing I am curious about is the reason for requiring $n+1$ SEPs. It seems to have something to do with MOs, and I will be posting about that in more detail in part 2!

Sources: https://chem.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Inorganic_Chemistry/Chemistry_of_the_Main_Group_Elements_(Barron)/06%3A_Group_13/6.05%3A_Wades_Rules

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyhedral_skeletal_electron_pair_theory

entry.title: torquoselectivity
entry.content:
By the Woodward-Hoffmann rules, a \(4\pi\) ring opening is conrotatory. However, for some asymmetrically substituted cyclobutenes, there is another type of selectivity that depends on which way the ring opens, called torquoselectivity. I originally thought this just progressed through sterics, i.e., the bulky group would rotate outwards, but it turns out that in 1984, the Houk group found some \(4\pi\) openings that do not do this. For example:

The left-hand product (Z) is favored despite the (E) product being thermodynamically favorable.

So what favors inward rotation?

As we can see, the HOMO has \(\sigma\) character, and the LUMO has \(\sigma^*\) character and can interact with substituents’ p-orbitals.

The figure shows the frontier orbitals in the transition state, with possible substituent locations.

What happens if the substituent rotates inward?

As we can see, the substituent will stabilize the HOMO and destabilize the LUMO. Thus, electron-donating substituents will tend to rotate outwards because of the destabilizing interaction with the LUMO. Conversely, acceptor substituents will rotate inwards due to the stabilizing interaction with the HOMO. (The LUMOs are empty, so there is no destabilizing interaction).

Sources: https://chemistry.stackexchange.com/questions/81188/stereoelectronic-effects-in-torquoselectivity-of-4%CF%80-electrocyclic-opening

Rondan, N. G.; Houk, K. N. Theory of stereoselection in conrotatory electrocyclic reactions of substituted cyclobutenes. J. Am. Chem. Soc. 1985, 107 (7), 2099–2111. DOI: 10.1021/ja00293a046
